sections.html:
Luzerne County's seat sits on a floodplain along the Susquehanna River. The city counts 44,523 residents and 16,644 households, a gain of 0.4 percent since April 2020. Roughly 51 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Typical values: a house at $117,200, monthly rent at $946, household income at $48,515.

With prices this modest, a fast as-is sale appeals to plenty of owners. The city adds one cost that most of the county escapes, a heavier transfer tax.

A deed for a Wilkes-Barre property carries 3.5 percent in total transfer tax. Most Luzerne County municipalities charge 2 percent. Recording waits on payment. Many contracts split the bill down the middle, yet the state can pursue either party for all of it, so a seller should not assume the buyer's side covers it.

Total realty transfer tax by location
LocationTotal rate
Most Luzerne County municipalities2% (1% state, 0.5% municipality, 0.5% school district)
Wilkes-Barre City3.5%
Pittston City3.5%
Kingston Borough2.5%
Hazleton City2%

Work out your net with the city rate before comparing offers, and put the split in writing.

sections.h2: Recording fees and the Recorder's office
sections.html:
The minimum to record a deed is $87.75, which includes four pages, four names and one parcel number. Beyond that, add $2.00 a page, $0.50 a name and $0.50 a parcel number.

  • The Recorder is at 200 North River Street, open 9:00 A.M. to 4:20 P.M. Call 570-825-1641 or 570-825-1642 with questions.
  • The buyer's certified address must be signed and attached to every deed. The county Assessor's Office certifies parcel numbers and charges a fee of its own.
  • A Statement of Value is required if less than the full tax is paid or an exemption is claimed. File an original and a copy. It is billed like an extra page, at $2.00.
  • Gifts of a house among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings are normally exempt, with the reason written on the deed.

The counter is for filing only. Questions about law, tax or title belong with your closing agent or an attorney.

Buyers ask about both. Tropical Storm Agnes in 1972 pushed the Susquehanna to nearly 41 feet, and downtown flooded under nine feet of water. The city then built a levee system rising 41 feet, finished in January 2003. The river set a record in September 2011, cresting at 42.66 feet, and the Wilkes-Barre levees held.

Mine subsidence is the quieter issue. Standard homeowner policies usually leave out damage from collapsed underground coal and clay mines. The state sells separate mine subsidence insurance through its Department of Environmental Protection, for example $150,000 of residential coverage at $41.25 a year. An online risk map shows whether an address sits over old workings.

Look up your street on the map before listing, and share the result with your buyer. A seller can cancel a policy at closing, and new owners must apply for their own.

A house that sits unused still costs money every month. Median monthly owner costs run $1,272 with a mortgage and $559 without one, and a second house is a real strain for many families.

  • A vacant house still draws a tax bill and a utility bill each month.
  • Floodplain location may raise insurance questions, so keep flood and mine subsidence paperwork together for the buyer.
  • Estates need proof of authority before anyone can sign a deed. A family transfer may be exempt from tax while a sale is not.
  • Tenants in place mean inspections and notices, so line up access dates in the contract.

Selling as-is for cash means no showings and no haggling over repairs. Still, weigh it against a listing by working out your own net after the city's 3.5 percent transfer tax and the recording fees.

Many Wilkes-Barre sales begin with a relative's house. Before anyone signs a deed, the person acting for the estate needs proof of authority, such as the letters or court papers. A family transfer can be exempt from transfer tax while a sale is not, so the structure of the deal changes the bill.

Deal with utilities, insurance and open tax bills first, since an unoccupied house still generates all three. A property that stood empty will prompt buyer questions about the roof, basement and past water damage, so decide in advance what you will say.

Before choosing, request at least one written cash offer for your address and set it beside a realistic listing estimate. Subtract the 3.5 percent city transfer tax share you would owe, recording costs, repairs and the months of taxes and utilities you would carry while waiting for a buyer.

A listing can bring a higher price when the house is in decent shape, but it also brings showings, repair requests and a wait on a buyer's loan. Cash gives up some price to get speed and certainty. In a city where the midpoint value is $117,200, the cost of repairs can use up much of what a polished listing would add, so price the repairs honestly before you decide.

sections.h2: What to ask the city before you list
sections.html:
Phone Wilkes-Barre City code enforcement and ask if your kind of property needs a certificate of occupancy, a rental license or a buyer notice before closing. Rules for rentals and occupied buildings differ from owner-occupied homes, and the office can tell you what an inspection covers and how long it takes.

Have the parcel number and the names on the deed handy, plus the letters or court papers showing who may sign if it is an estate. If liens or back taxes exist, request payoff figures early. An as-is purchaser can often work around those items, but the seller still has to hand over a deed the Recorder will accept.

After you accept an offer, order payoff figures, get the parcel number certified and collect the buyer's certified address for the deed. Your closing agent drafts the deed and any Statement of Value and carries both, with payment, to the Recorder. The deed is indexed and the tax settled in one visit.

With a cash buyer there is usually no lender appraisal or loan approval, so the closing date turns on title work and any city paperwork. Ask each buyer for a written offer, a closing date and proof of funds, and ask who pays recording costs and the city's share of transfer tax.

faqs.q: How high is the Wilkes-Barre transfer tax?
faqs.a: It is 3.5 percent in total for a property inside Wilkes-Barre City, against 2 percent in most Luzerne County municipalities. Buyer and seller usually split it, and the deed cannot be recorded until it is paid.

faqs.q: Who records the deed after a Wilkes-Barre sale?
faqs.a: The Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds, 200 North River Street, normally by way of your closing agent or title company. A deed starts at $87.75.

faqs.q: Is mine subsidence a concern for Wilkes-Barre homes?
faqs.a: It can be, because the region was heavily mined for anthracite. Check the state Department of Environmental Protection's online risk map for your address. Standard homeowner policies usually exclude this damage.

faqs.q: Must I fix a Wilkes-Barre house first?
faqs.a: No. Someone buying as-is takes the house with its problems. Occupancy or rental rules from the city may still apply, so ask code enforcement before you set a settlement day.

faqs.q: Are family transfers taxed in Luzerne County?
faqs.a: Spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings can generally transfer without the tax. State the relationship on the deed, and file a Statement of Value if you claim an exemption.
